claims.text: The magnetocaloric effect in non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys can be systematically tuned by varying composition using combinatorial thin-film deposition followed by annealing near the magnetic transition temperature.
The initial non-equiatomic HEA thin films have a random solid-solution structure.
The initial films are synthesized by combinatorial deposition.
Combinatorial thin-film deposition can introduce a composition gradient in HEA films.
Controlled annealing near the magnetic transition temperature can stabilize a desired HEA microstructure.
Applying controlled magnetic fields during annealing helps stabilize the desired microstructure.
The relevant experiments should be focused around a known magnetic-transition region.
Local variations in elemental ratios modify magnetic exchange interactions in the alloy.
Local variations in elemental ratios modify phase stability in the alloy.
Changing alloy composition alters the electronic configurations of the constituent elements.
Composition-dependent electronic and magnetic interactions shift the magnetic ordering temperature.
Composition changes modify the magneto-entropy landscape.
Modification of the magneto-entropy landscape changes the magnitude of the magnetocaloric effect.
A composition gradient will produce a systematic variation in magnetic transition temperature.
A composition gradient will produce a systematic variation in magnetic entropy change.
Some compositions will exhibit enhanced magnetocaloric properties relative to a uniform-composition baseline.
The approach is applicable to non-equiatomic HEAs for which controlled thin-film deposition and annealing are feasible.
Large compositional variations may induce phase separation.
Composition-induced phase separation may degrade the magnetocaloric response.
The composition range maximizing the magnetocaloric effect and the magnitude of enhancement remain unknown.
